# Job Chapter 22 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 424r–424v

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:

**2** "Can a man be profitable to God? Surely even a wise man is profitable only to himself. **3** Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are righteous, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless?

**4** Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you?

**5** Is not your wickedness great? There is no end to your iniquities.

**6** For you have exacted pledges from your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing. **7** You have given no water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry.

**8** The man with power possessed the land, and the favored man lived in it. **9** You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed.

**10** Therefore snares are all around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you, **11** or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of waters covers you.

**12** Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are!

**13** But you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness? **14** Thick clouds veil him so that he does not see, and he walks on the vault of heaven.'

**15** Will you keep to the old path that the wicked have trod? **16** They were snatched away before their time; their foundation was washed away by a flood.

**17** They said to God, 'Depart from us,' and 'What can the Almighty do to us?'

**18** Yet he filled their houses with good things — but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.

**19** The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent mock at them, **20** saying, 'Surely our foes are cut off, and what they left the fire has consumed.'

**21** Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you.

**22** Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.

**23** If you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents,

**24** if you lay your gold in the dust, and the gold of Ophir among the stones of the streams, **25** then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.

**26** For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God.

**27** You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows. **28** You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways.

**29** When they are brought low you will say, 'It is because of pride!' For he saves the humble.

**30** He delivers even the one who is not innocent, and that one will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands."

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Job 22 opens the third and final cycle of speeches (chs. 22-27). Eliphaz's third speech represents the full degradation of the friends' position. Where once he reasoned from personal revelation (ch. 4) and traditional wisdom (ch. 15), he now resorts to specific, fabricated accusations (vv.6-9). The theological logic that drives him is stated in vv.2-4: since human righteousness does not benefit God, God has no motive to punish the innocent. Therefore Job must be guilty. The syllogism is valid; the minor premise (that punishment always indicates guilt) is false. Ironically, Eliphaz's closing appeal (vv.21-30) contains some of the most beautiful devotional language in the book — "the Almighty will be your gold" (v.25), "he saves the humble" (v.29). The tragedy is that true theology has been built on a false diagnosis. Verse 30 carries deep irony: Eliphaz says the clean-handed person can intercede for the guilty. In the epilogue (42:7-9), this is exactly what happens — but it is Job who intercedes for Eliphaz, not the other way around.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.2 — "profitable to God" vs. "of any use to God"
- **EMET:** "Can-a-man be-profitable to-God?"
- **LOGOS:** "Can a man be profitable to God?"
- **PNEUMA:** "Can a human being be of any use to God?"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Can a man be profitable to God?" — the Hebrew *yiskon* (from *sakan*, to be of use/profit) carries economic connotation. "Profitable" preserves this better than PNEUMA's general "of any use."

### V.8 — Who is "the man with power"?
- **EMET:** "the-man of-arm — to-him is the-land"
- **LOGOS:** "The man with power possessed the land"
- **PNEUMA:** "You thought the land belonged to the powerful"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "The man with power possessed the land, and the favored man lived in it" — this proverb-like statement is spoken by Eliphaz as part of his accusation. PNEUMA turns it into Job's alleged inner thought ("you thought"), which adds interpretation. The statement should stand as Eliphaz's description of the social order Job allegedly endorsed.

### V.29 — "It is because of pride" vs. "Lift them up"
- **EMET:** "you-will-say, 'Lifting-up! [gevah]'"
- **LOGOS:** "you will say, 'It is because of pride!'"
- **PNEUMA:** "you will say, 'Lift them up!'"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "you will say, 'It is because of pride!' For he saves the humble." The Hebrew *gevah* means "height/pride/lifting up." In context, Eliphaz is contrasting pride with humility: when people are brought low, the restored Job will recognize that it is pride that causes downfall, and God saves the humble. PNEUMA's "lift them up" reads *gevah* as an imperative, which is grammatically possible but less likely in context.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
